distr::Gamma¶

The gamma distribution: a flexible family on the positive axis, the sum of exponential waiting times and the parent of the chi-squared family.

Signature¶

pluss::Series distr::pdf(dst::Gamma, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::logpdf(dst::Gamma, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::cdf(dst::Gamma, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::logcdf(dst::Gamma, const pluss::Series& x, const std::vector<double>& params);
pluss::Series distr::sample(dst::Gamma, const std::vector<double>& params, std::initializer_list<std::int64_t> sizes, pluss::Config cfg = {}, std::uint64_t seed = 0);

What It Does¶

The gamma distribution is the distribution of the waiting time until the shape-th event of a Poisson process, and more generally a flexible model for positive, right-skewed quantities such as rainfall amounts, claim sizes and service times. Its mean is shape × scale and its variance shape × scale². With shape = 1 it is the exponential distribution, with integer shape the Erlang distribution, and with shape = ν/2 and scale = 2 the chi-squared distribution with ν degrees of freedom.

The kind-based functions take {shape} (scale 1, location 0) or the long form {location, scale, shape}, note the order. The object distr::Gamma{shape, scale, location} has the order shape, scale, location.

The parameters, in the order of the params list:

Parameter

Constraint

Meaning

location

any real

the left end of the support (0 in the short form)

scale

> 0

stretches the axis; the mean is shape × scale

shape

> 0

controls the skewness: small values pile up near the location, large values approach a bell shape

Support: x above the location.

The object form of this family, with the same functions as methods, is on its own page: distr::Gamma.

Parameters¶

const pluss::Series& x

The points at which to evaluate, a Series of any shape; the result has the same shape. Points outside the support have density zero and distribution value 0 or 1.

const std::vector<double>& params

The parameters of the family, in the order shown in the table above (a shorter list selects the defaults: {shape} gives scale 1 and location 0). A list of the wrong length is refused.

std::initializer_list<std::int64_t> sizes

The shape of the array of random draws, for example {n} or {rows, columns}.

pluss::Config cfg

The dtype and platform of the draws; the default is Float32 on the CPU, so request Float64 when precision matters.

std::uint64_t seed

The seed of the stream. The same seed always gives the same draws; a seed of 0 is a fixed default, not a random one.

Returns¶

pdf, logpdf, cdf and logcdf return a Series of the shape of x; sample returns a Series of the requested shape.

Errors¶

  • Parameters outside their valid range are refused with an error that names the requirement (shape and scale must be positive).

  • A params list of the wrong length is refused.

Practical Examples¶

Example 1¶

Example 1 evaluates the density (mass) function, the distribution function and the log-density of the Gamma on a small grid with distr::pdf, distr::cdf and distr::logpdf.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(5);

  const auto x = pluss::make_series({0.25, 1.0, 2.0, 3.5, 6.0, 10.0}, f64);
  const std::vector<double> params = {0.0, 1.3, 2.5};

  std::cout << "x:";
  for (double v : x.pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "pdf:";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::Gamma, x, params).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "cdf:";
  for (double v : distr::cdf(dst::Gamma, x, params).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "logpdf:";
  for (double v : distr::logpdf(dst::Gamma, x, params).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
}

Output

x: 0.25000 1.00000 2.00000 3.50000 6.00000 10.00000
pdf: 0.04026 0.18090 0.23709 0.17312 0.05679 0.00563
cdf: 0.00426 0.09141 0.31187 0.62924 0.89979 0.99116
logpdf: -3.21234 -1.70982 -1.43933 -1.75376 -2.86834 -5.17902

The density is largest on this grid at x = 2, where it is 0.23709; the distribution function runs from 0.00426 at x = 0.25 to 0.99116 at x = 10, and it is the running total of the density. logpdf is the logarithm of the density, for example log(0.23709) = -1.43932 at x = 2.

Example 2¶

Example 2 checks that the three descriptions of the same probability agree: the integral of the density (sum of the masses) over a range, the difference of the distribution function at its ends, and the fraction of random draws that land in it.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(5);
  const std::vector<double> params = {0.0, 1.3, 2.5};

  // The three ways to the probability that the variable lies in [1, 6]:
  const auto grid = pluss::series::linspace(1.0, 6.0, 3001, f64);
  const double area = as_f64(distr::pdf(dst::Gamma, grid, params).antidiff(grid).trapezoid());

  const auto edges = pluss::make_series({1.0, 6.0}, f64);
  const auto c = distr::cdf(dst::Gamma, edges, params).pull<double>();

  const auto draws = distr::sample(dst::Gamma, params, {200000}, f64, 7ULL);
  const double fraction = as_f64(((draws >= 1.0).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64) * (draws <= 6.0).to(pluss::ScalarType::Float64)).mean());

  std::cout << "integral of the density: " << area << '\n';
  std::cout << "cdf(6) - cdf(1): " << c[1] - c[0] << '\n';
  std::cout << "fraction of 200000 draws in range: " << fraction << '\n';
}

Output

integral of the density: 0.80838
cdf(6) - cdf(1): 0.80838
fraction of 200000 draws in range: 0.80714

The integral of the density (0.80838) and the difference of the distribution function (0.80838) agree to all printed digits: they are two computations of one probability. The fraction of random draws (0.80714) differs from it by 0.00124, which is the size of the sampling error of a fraction of 200000 draws (a standard error of about 8.80e-04), so the density, the distribution function and the sampler describe the same distribution.

Example 3¶

Example 3 shows how the shape changes with the parameters: the density at the same points for 3 parameter settings.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({0.25, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0, 14.0}, f64);

  std::cout << "x:";
  for (double v : x.pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "shape 0.8:";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::Gamma, x, {0.0, 1.3, 0.8}).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "shape 2.5:";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::Gamma, x, {0.0, 1.3, 2.5}).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
  std::cout << "shape 8  :";
  for (double v : distr::pdf(dst::Gamma, x, {0.0, 1.3, 8.0}).pull<double>()) std::cout << ' ' << v;
  std::cout << '\n';
}

Output

x: 0.2500 1.0000 2.0000 4.0000 8.0000 14.0000
shape 0.8: 0.7581 0.3227 0.1302 0.0243 0.0010 0.0000
shape 2.5: 0.0403 0.1809 0.2371 0.1440 0.0188 0.0004
shape 8  : 0.0000 0.0000 0.0007 0.0184 0.1084 0.0539

Read down the rows: shape 0.8 peaks on this grid at x = 0.25 (value 0.7581); shape 2.5 peaks on this grid at x = 2 (value 0.2371); shape 8 peaks on this grid at x = 8 (value 0.1084). The parameters move the location, the width and the shape of the curve, which is what choosing a member of the family means.

Example 4¶

Example 4 confirms that the chi-squared distribution with 5 degrees of freedom is a gamma with shape 2.5 and scale 2.

#include <pluss/ma.h>

#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

namespace distr = pluss::subsp::stats::distr;
namespace dst = distr::dst;

int main() {
  const auto f64 = pluss::Config{}.with_dtype(pluss::ScalarType::Float64);
  std::cout << std::scientific << std::setprecision(2);
  const auto x = pluss::make_series({0.5, 1.5, 3.0, 6.0, 12.0}, f64);
  const std::vector<double> here = {0.0, 2.0, 2.5};
  const std::vector<double> there = {5.0};

  const double dpdf = as_f64((distr::pdf(dst::Gamma, x, here) - distr::pdf(dst::ChiSquare, x, there)).abs().max());
  const double dcdf = as_f64((distr::cdf(dst::Gamma, x, here) - distr::cdf(dst::ChiSquare, x, there)).abs().max());
  std::cout << "largest difference in the density: " << dpdf << '\n';
  std::cout << "largest difference in the distribution function: " << dcdf << '\n';
}

Output

largest difference in the density: 0.00e+00
largest difference in the distribution function: 0.00e+00

The two largest differences are 0 for the density and 0 for the distribution function over the grid: zero up to rounding, so the two descriptions are the same distribution.
